summary: This excerpt from Kate Douglas Wiggin's novel (Book 11, part 21) opens with a child's letter to John about a dog, the barn, and paying off a mortgage, then shows Rebecca starting school at Riverboro Centre. Miss Sawyer arranges Rebecca's enrollment with teacher Miss Dearborn, who has no special training. The passage then follows Rebecca's daily walk through woods and pastures, full of vivid natural detail.
one_line: Rebecca begins school at Riverboro Centre under Miss Dearborn and walks a woodland short cut each morning.
key_facts: Rebecca's arrival had been on a Friday, and on the following Monday she began her education at the school in Riverboro Centre, about a mile distant.
Miss Sawyer borrowed a neighbor's horse and wagon to drive Rebecca to the schoolhouse.
Miss Sawyer interviewed the teacher, Miss Dearborn, arranged for books, and started Rebecca's education.
Miss Dearborn had had no special preparation in the art of teaching; her family said teaching came to her naturally.
The narrator compares Miss Dearborn to Tom Tulliver's clergyman tutor, who taught with uniformity of method and independence of circumstances.
The narrator compares Miss Dearborn's methods to a beaver that builds a dam in a London room as earnestly as in a lake in Upper Canada.
Rebecca walked to school after the first morning and loved this part of the day.
On fair days with light dew, Rebecca took a short cut through the woods.
Her route crossed uncle Josh Woodman's bars, passed Mrs. Carter's cows, and crossed a woodland brook by jumping from stone to stone.
In the woods she saw fungous growths of brilliant orange and crimson and clumps of waxen Indian pipes.
The letter from Rebecca to John says the brick house is the barn and that she cannot bite Aunt M. because she must be grateful.
The letter says education is going to be the making of Rebecca and will help John pay off the mortgage when they grow up.
The letter mentions that the Simpsons are mortgaged, while Richard Carter and Dr. Winship are not.
